messages.body_plain:
Hi Jay.

Try:

chp<-getChipEffectSet(plm)

readUnits(plm,units=1) will give you the chip effects (i.e.
expression levels).

To get it in matrix format, either you can 'unwrap' the list
structure that readUnits returns or you can use the 'extractMatrix'
function.

Awhile ago, I made a function to get the expression values from the
chip effect set, that may be useful for you.  See below.  You would
run it as:

d<-getExprs(chp)

... and then you could write.table that to a file if you wanted.

getExprs <- function(ces, ...) {
   cdf <- getCdf(ces);
   theta <- extractMatrix(ces, ..., returnUgcMap=TRUE);
   ugcMap <- attr(theta, "unitGroupCellMap");
   un<-getUnitNames(cdf, ugcMap[,"unit"]);
   rownames(theta) <- un
   log2(theta)
}

Cheers,
Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi J.

Are you using the Ensembl CDF from the google website?  If so, the
rownames of theta should be 'ENSGXXX' already ... note that this is
NOT the first column of theta ... though if you write it to a text
file with row.names=T, then it'll be the first column there.

If you are getting transcript_cluster_ids, then I'm a bit confused as
to how you've processed the data.  Maybe give me you're entire list
of commands, or at least a 'print(csN)' and a 'print(getCdf(csN))' ...

As far as transforming to ENST labels, there is a subtle point here.
The CDF file has been generated as 'gene-centric', which basically
means that all the probes for a give GENE (i.e. all known transcripts
if more than one) are treated as one unit.  If you want individual
transcript estimates, that's a different question and not one that I
have addressed.  Maybe someone else on the list has.  But, if
differential splicing is what you are after, then I'd suggest trying
FIRMA (see google page).

Hope that helps.
Mark

> Ok, it is obvious you've done your homework and found how to
> circumvent the default behavior of not accepting ASCII CDFs.  The
> intention of actually having this option is to leave a final resort to
> turn to if you cannot get/generate a binary CDF for one reason or the
> other.  However, you should always going to strive to use a binary
> CDF.  Using an ASCII CDF is going to be painfully slow and consume
> much more memory.
>
> In your case you should be able to create a binary version of your CDF
> by using convertCdf() in affxparser, e.g.
>
> convertCdf(srcPathname, destPathname)
>
> Note that the ASCII and the binary CDF will/must have the same
> filename, e.g. HG-U133A.cdf.  So, make sure to put away the ASCII and
> instead have the binary in
> annotationData/chipTypes/HG-U133A/HG-U133A.cdf.  Do the same for the
> HG-U133B.cdf.  If you do print(cdf) you will see if aroma.affymetrix
> finds the ASCII or the binary CDF.
>
> > ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A",
> > checkChipType=FALSE);
> > qn <- QuantileNormalization(ds);
> > csQN <- process(qn,verbose=TRUE);

> AffymetrixCelSet:
> Name: myDataSet
> Tags:
> Path: rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133A
> Chip type: HG-U133A
> Number of arrays: 5896
> Names: 1102960533, 1102960569, ..., GSM9934
> Time period: 2001-01-01 10:13:54 -- NA
> Total file size: 78459.64MB
> RAM: 6.21MB
>
> So, the reason for the slow processing here is that the print()
> function for an AffymetrixCelSet reports the time period of the first
> and the last time stamp of the CEL files.  In order to figure this
> out, it has to query and parse the CEL header of every single CEL
> file.  This is something I've anticipated would happen, but I've
> procrastinating optimizing it until it became a real issue, which it
> now is.  Obviously, we do not want to do this if it takes to long.  I
> can image adding an option that allows you to specify the maximum
> number of arrays to report the time period, otherwise it will not be
> reported.
>
>
>
> > 4) I tried using both verbose and verbatim.  Same results.

>
>

> > However, without the settings and checkChipType changes in step 2, the
> > code complains about finding two chipTypes, so maybe there are indeed
> > two types of chips.
>
> The 'checkChipType' will scan *all* CEL files and assert that the chip
> type is the same for all and match the name of the parent directory of
> the CEL files, e.g. "HG-U133A" in your rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133A/
> case.  This is to prevent mistakes, which obviously can happen for
> many reasons.  As above, since this queries every single CEL file
> having checkChipType=TRUE will take some time with your data set.
>
> Which two chip types did it report - HG-U133A and HG-U133B?
>
> You should never put CEL files of different chip types (think
> different physical chip types that are produced by Affymetrix) in the
> same directory.  Instead, in your case put the CEL files of the two
> types in separated directories;
>
> rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133A/
> rawData/myDataSet/HG-U133B/
>
> Then you have to treat to to sets of CELs as different data sets for
> normalization, summarization and post-normalization.  It is first when
> you get the final normalized summarized signals (chip effects) that
> you can start thinking how to combine the two sets.  I know that there
> are some discussion on normalizing the two chip types together using
> common genes, but there is nothing available out of the box in
> aroma.affymetrix.
>
> The error message you get from running the quantile normalization
> might be due to the fact that you mix up the two chip types.  I will
> leave it for now until you retry doing it on the two chip types
> separately, ok?
>
> I will put it on my todo list to add additional speed optimization
> methods for >1000 array data sets.  I already now have some ideas on
> how to better cache CEL headers, since they are reread multiple times.
>
> Hope this helps
>
> Henrik

> > files).

That's good.

> >
> > However, the other group (4000+) still complains about having 2 CEL
> > chip types.  How does your code check for the chip types?  What
> > particular parameter in the CEL file header does not use to determine
> > chip types?

The validation/check is done by comparing the chip type according to
the CEL file header.  In other words, one or more CEL files reports a
chip type in the file header different from the main chip type.

It will help if you let me know what the two chip types
aroma.affymetrix is reporting.  I don't believe there is a bug in
aroma.affymetrix causing the problem, but rather there is something
odd with you set of CEL files.  For some chip types, Affymetrix have
used different names over the time although the chip is identical.
But, I cannot really tell what the problem is unless I have more
details.

You can also do something like:

ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A",
checkChipType=FALSE);

allChipTypes <- unlist(lapply(ds, FUN=getChipType))
table(allChipTypes)

to find out how many CEL files you have of each chip type.

Hope this helps

/Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

Ok, first thing I observe when I compare the two files, is that
'GSM123182.cel' is of file format v4 (binary) and 'GSM123184.cel' is
of file format v3 (ASCII).  I then note that the ASCII file works, but
not the binary.  I also note that it is not only then chip type that
is not correct, but all of the CEL header is blank.  I have never
heard of something similar before.  Have the binary CEL files been
converted from ASCII-to-binary by some tool?

If you could zip the two CEL files and make the available to me
somewhere so that I can download them, I could also have a look at
them.

Comment: You do indeed want to work with binary files (since ASCII is
slower and more memory-hungry to work with), although if you do for
instance quantile normalization on ASCII CEL files, the normalized
data is stored as binary CEL files, so you can "live with" having raw
data in the ASCII format.

/Henrik

> These CEL files are all received AS IS without any ASCII-to-binary
> conversion.  Does affyparser not parse binary format files?

Ok, both files are indeed in ASCII file format.  The 'affxparser' is
using the Affymetrix Fusion SDK library internally.  The latter does
parse all CEL/CDF file formats released by Affymetrix and since it is
used in many other software by many other users, we are rather
confident that it does the right thing, especially when it comes to
the common CEL and CDF formats.

This is the problem.  If you look at the two CEL files in a text
editor on a non-Windows system or in a text editor that is not written
by Microsoft, you will see that 'GSM123182.cel' have extra carriage
returns that should not be there between every row.  You can also see
this like this:

> readChar("GSM123182.cel", n=30)
[1] "[CEL]\r\r\nVersion=3\r\r\n\r\r\n[HEADER"
> readChar("GSM123184.cel", n=30)
[1] "[CEL]\r\nVersion=3\r\n\r\n[HEADER]\r\n"

Note the difference.  There is an extra '\r' in the former.  I
strongly suspect that this has happened because either i) those files
were downloaded via FTP in a non-binary mode (classical mistake) or
ii) someone have edited those files manually (most likely on an old
Mac OS v9 or before, cf http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newline).

You will need to remove all those errounous carriage returns in those
files, because as it is now, those CEL files does not comply with the
defined file format.  Be care to backup your files so you keep the
originals in case something goes wrong while correcting the files.
You might be able to do something like:

library(aroma.affymetrix);
mkdirs("fixed");
pathname <- "GSM123184.cel";
raw <- readBin(con=pathname, what="raw", n=file.info <http://file.info>(pathname)$size);
raw2 <- raw[raw != charToRaw("\r")];
pathname2 <- file.path("fixed", basename(pathname));
writeBin(con=pathname2, raw2);
hdr <- readCelHeader(pathname2);
> str(hdr)
List of 12
 $ filename  : chr "fixed/GSM123184.cel"
 $ version   : int 3
 $ cols      : int 712
 $ rows      : int 712
 $ total     : int 506944
 $ algorithm : chr "Percentile"
 $ parameters: chr "Percentile:75;CellMargin:2;OutlierHigh:1.500;OutlierLow:1.00
4"
 $ chiptype  : chr "HG-U133A"
 $ header    : chr "Cols=712\nRows=712\nTotalX=712\nTotalY=712\nOffsetX=0\nOffse
tY=0\nGridCornerUL=229 232\nGridCornerUR=4499 249\nGridCornerLR=448"| __truncate
d__
 $ cellmargin: int 2
 $ noutliers : int 4340
 $ nmasked   : int 0

Hope this helps

Henrik

> > These CEL files are all received AS IS without any ASCII-to-binary
> > conversion.  Does affyparser not parse binary format files?
>
> Ok, both files are indeed in ASCII file format.  The 'affxparser' is
> using the Affymetrix Fusion SDK library internally.  The latter does
> parse all CEL/CDF file formats released by Affymetrix and since it is
> used in many other software by many other users, we are rather
> confident that it does the right thing, especially when it comes to
> the common CEL and CDF formats.
>
> This is the problem.  If you look at the two CEL files in a text
> editor on a non-Windows system or in a text editor that is not written
> by Microsoft, you will see that 'GSM123182.cel' have extra carriage
> returns that should not be there between every row.  You can also see
> this like this:
>
> > readChar("GSM123182.cel", n=30)
> [1] "[CEL]\r\r\nVersion=3\r\r\n\r\r\n[HEADER"
> > readChar("GSM123184.cel", n=30)
> [1] "[CEL]\r\nVersion=3\r\n\r\n[HEADER]\r\n"
>
> Note the difference.  There is an extra '\r' in the former.  I
> strongly suspect that this has happened because either i) those files
> were downloaded via FTP in a non-binary mode (classical mistake) or
> ii) someone have edited those files manually (most likely on an old
> Mac OS v9 or before, cf http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newline).
>
> You will need to remove all those errounous carriage returns in those
> files, because as it is now, those CEL files does not comply with the
> defined file format.  Be care to backup your files so you keep the
> originals in case something goes wrong while correcting the files.
> You might be able to do something like:
>
> library(aroma.affymetrix);
> mkdirs("fixed");
> pathname <- "GSM123184.cel";
> raw <- readBin(con=pathname, what="raw", n=file.info <http://file.info>(pathname)$size);
> raw2 <- raw[raw != charToRaw("\r")];
> pathname2 <- file.path("fixed", basename(pathname));

> hdr <- readCelHeader(pathname2);
> > str(hdr)

Hi all,
There is also a function that returns the group names
(readCdfGroupNames) from a cdf, basically like Mark's suggested code.
I've done code something like this before:

plmNoMergeTissue<- ExonRmaPlm(csNTissue, mergeGroups=FALSE)
cesNoMergeTissue<-getChipEffectSet(plmNoMergeTissue)
pbsetSumm<-extractMatrix(cesNoMergeTissue,returnUgcMap=TRUE,units=1:3)
#or whatever units you want
pbsetNames<-readCdfGroupNames(getPathname(getCdf(cesNoMergeTissue)),unit=1:3)
rownames(pbsetSumm)<-unlist(pbsetNames)

Note that I use the cdf of cesNoMergeTissue, which is the monocell cdf
with one entry per group allowed, and not the original cdf.

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I've been working on two methods to help out here.  They will probably
show up in the next release.  In the meantime, you can grab them as
patches, i.e. just do once:

  downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")

The methods work like this:

> data <- extractDataFrame(ces, units=312:314)
> str(data)
'data.frame':   31 obs. of  7 variables:
 $ unit                 : int  312 312 312 312 312 312 312 312 ...
 $ group                : int  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ...
 $ cell                 : int  4775 4776 4777 4778 4779 4780 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_A: num   7.01 36.82 18.47 23.75 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_B: num   7.52 56.99 14.51 29.31 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_C: num   6.73 40.53 13.58 16.59 ...
 $ huex_wta_heart_A     : num    6.72  57.15  97.25  77.89 ...

So when extract data as a data.frame the (unit,group,cell) map is
contained in the first three columns.  The rest of the columns are the
names of the arrays.  extractDataFrame() calls extractMatrix()
internally and takes the same arguments.

> ugpMap <- data[,c("unit", "group", "cell")]
> ugNames <- getUnitGroupNamesFromUgcMap(getCdf(ces), ugcMap=ugcMap)
> data <- cbind(ugNames, data)
> str(data)
'data.frame':   31 obs. of  9 variables:
 $ unitName             : chr  "2336706" "2336706" "2336706" ...
 $ groupName            : chr  "2336712" "2336713" "2336714" ...
 $ unit                 : int  312 312 312 312 312 312 312 312 ...
 $ group                : int  1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 ...
 $ cell                 : int  4775 4776 4777 4778 4779 4780 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_A: num   7.01 36.82 18.47 23.75 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_B: num   7.52 56.99 14.51 29.31 ...
 $ huex_wta_cerebellum_C: num   6.73 40.53 13.58 16.59 ...
 $ huex_wta_heart_A     : num    6.72  57.15  97.25  77.89 ...

The above methods should work in all cases regardless of value on
'mergeGroups' and similar arguments that select a subset of the
groups.  (I might consider adding an argument 'addNames' to
extractDataFrame() to encapsulate the latter method call).

Let me know if works as expected

/Henrik

messages.subject: Re: Erroneous CEL files? (Was:Re: Analyzing >1000 HG-U133A/B arrays)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Henrik,

You nailed the problem (the extra \r in the faulty files).  So we used
a little script (outside R) to get all the files fixed in batch mode.
It turned out that among 5896 cel files, only a handful (31) are
affected.  We also had to filter out the [MODIFIED] section in the cel
files since they do contain valid (maybe) \r\r markers.

Here is the little bash script that does the job, for future
reference.

ls | xargs -n 1 bash -c 'perl -ne "if (1../\[MODIFIED\]/) { if (/\\r\\r
$/) { print \"`echo $1`\n\"; exit() }}" $1' -- | xargs -n 1 perl -
i.bak -pe 's/\r\r$//'

Now we are happily on the QN part.  It has been 20 hours since the
processing started, and now it is running on the 4200th chip.  The
memory usage is about 560M so far, very impressive.

I will keep you posted on the results.

Dong

On Feb 7, 2008 11:52 AM, Dong Fu <dongf...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Henrik,
>
> You nailed the problem (the extra \r in the faulty files).  So we used
> a little script (outside R) to get all the files fixed in batch mode.
> It turned out that among 5896 cel files, only a handful (31) are
> affected.  We also had to filter out the [MODIFIED] section in the cel
> files since they do contain valid (maybe) \r\r markers.
>
> Here is the little bash script that does the job, for future
> reference.
>
> ls | xargs -n 1 bash -c 'perl -ne "if (1../\[MODIFIED\]/) { if (/\\r\\r
> $/) { print \"`echo $1`\n\"; exit() }}" $1' -- | xargs -n 1 perl -
> i.bak -pe 's/\r\r$//'

Thanks for sharing this.

>
> Now we are happily on the QN part.  It has been 20 hours since the
> processing started, and now it is running on the 4200th chip.  The
> memory usage is about 560M so far, very impressive.

I'm glad to hear that is working for you know.

To the best of my knowledge this is the first time aroma.affymetrix is
used to process 1000+ arrays and it is good to see that memory usage
is (almost) constant; the trick is to design the QN algorithm to do a
two-pass scan of data, so that it only has to hold the target signals
and the signal from one array in memory at any time.  You'll find all
details in:

H. Bengtsson; R. Irizarry; B. Carvalho; T.P. Speed, Estimation and
assessment of raw copy numbers at the single locus level,
Bioinformatics 2008. [pmid: 18204055]

>
> I will keep you posted on the results.

My next concern is that when fitting the log-additive model (as in
RMA), if that is what you plan, the processing time is exponential(?)
in the number of probes.  This is something that have bitten a few
processing exon array data using the default Affymetrix CDF.  You can
find studies on this on Page "Optimization (Speed, file space & RAM)":

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/optimization-speed-file-space-ram

Since the log-additive model is symmetric in probes and samples (it is
basically just fitting additive effects across rows and columns in a
matrix), the same applies when having a large number of samples.
However, note the comment that Ben Bolstad made - the penalty for
having a large number of samples is smaller than the penalty for
having a large number of probes, which is good in your case.

I guess we have to wait and see what happens.  I'm keen to hear what
you observe.

/Henrik

Hello Henrik,

Do you ever rest and not respond so quickly?  :-)  Just kidding.

Once the QN is finished, we will do the RMAPLM on it.

Just for reference.  We ran the same steps on about 1500 arrays last
week.  The QN took about 10 hours, and the RMAPLM took about 20
hours.  The memory usage during the calculation was very constant at
around 500MB.

The only wish I have is for R to take advantage of the multi-core/
multi-CPU capability at a more fundamental level.  Right now it is
using only 1 CPU 100% while the rest of the CPUs are idling.  I could
try using the fork package, but with the stringent requirement of

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have been trying to get out the RLE and NUSE values (not the boxplot
summaries) and so copied the code from the plotNuse and plotRle
commands, and I think there's a problem for the ExonRmaPlm model (for
merge=T). Below is what I think replicates the plotRle code (for
example) if subset=NULL, except instead of doing getData for each file
separately, I'm getting them as one singe matrix.

cesEnsbGBM<-getChipEffects(plmEnsbGBM)
cdfMonoEnsb<-getCdf(cesEnsbGBM)
nbrOfUnits<-nbrOfUnits(cdfMonoEnsb)
units<-1:nbrOfUnits
avgLE <- getAverageLog(cesEnsbGBM, field = "intensities", indices =
NULL, verbose = verbose)
medianLE <- getData(avgLE, indices = units, "intensities")$intensities
medianLE <- log2(medianLE)
rleGBM <- getData(cesEnsbGBM, indices = units,"intensities")
$intensities
rleGBM <- log2(rleGBM)
rleGBM <- rleGBM-medianLE

Then for avgLE, I get -Inf values (after the log2); I think they
correspond to the 'blank' storage places (with merge=T, only 1 of the
group slots stores anything and the rest are blank). Unlike the
extractMatrix commands, it's not weeding out these blank storage
places. I don't know an elegant way to fix this. I'm just going to do
indices for the -Inf values and weed them out that way.

If I'm correct, this seriously effects our interpretation of what
we've been plotting for quality control!

Best,
Elizabeth

On Feb 8, 2008 12:55 PM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi anyone (probably Henrik),
>
> I was using the subset option in plotDensity, and I wanted to confirm
> that if I say subset=1/2 it doesn't give me a *random* subset of the probes.
>
> I say this because I looked at the code for identifyCells, and this
> seems to be how the probes are picked:
>
>         if (getFraction) {
>              indices <- other[seq(from = 1, to = length(other),
>                  by = by)]
>          }
>
> which means they are equally spaced in the order of the cdf.
>
> I'm not entirely clear on the behavior of 'subset'. If I wanted to give
> an vector argument to subset, it should be between 1 and number of Cells
> on cdf, right? If I choose type="pm", would it only do the pm ones of
> the one I gave to subset, or all (ignoring type="pm')
>
> (By accident, I did subset=1/2 on quantile normalized data and get a set
> of arrays (corresponding to a particular batch...) that have fairly
> different density plots so I am trying to decide whether that should
> worry me)

Yes, you are right that the 'subset' argument is internally passed
down as identifyCells(..., indices=subset) for AffymetrixCdfFile.
Then, the 'indices' argument of identifyCells() is interpreted in
either of two ways.  If it is a single numeric value in (0,1) (soft
boundaries), it is interpreted as a fraction, that is, it will return
that fraction of cells.  The returned cells are uniformly distributed
from the first to the last cell, as your code snippet shows.  If
'indices' is a vector of numeric (or the single value 1), it will be
interpreted exactly as the cells you want.

If you want to get a random subset of a certain fraction of all cells,
you have to generate that yourself and pass it as a vector.

/Henrik

>
> Best,
> Elizabeth
>
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jay,

ExonRmaPlm is a class for fitting the probe-level model, only. The
background correction and normalization are done before hand (see the
example on the help pages) -- there's not a single command that does the
whole 'vanilla' RMA processing. The standard background correction is
done with RmaBackgroundCorrection. I assume you are wanting a gc-RMA
background correction. There is a gcRMA background correction function
(GcRmaBackgroundCorrection). But I believe out-of-the-box gc correction
uses MM probes, so I don't know that you would want to use this function
for exon arrays. But I know nothing much about the function.

Note there are some 'MM' probes classified in Affy's cdf. I've never
understood what they are. I know that there are many probes on the array
for background correction that could be used for this purpose, and maybe
Affy has labeled them 'MM'. I've never had a chance to work it out. But
again, I think there would have to be a specially created function to do
this...

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was just wondering, if I am frequently changing the cdf for a
AffymetrixCelSet am I going to run into any problems with something that
has been cached? Is it better to make duplicate objects with their own
cdf? setCdf(cs,cdf) actually takes a bit of time, so it's probably
better for that reason.

Similarly, if I call setCdf(cs,cdf) within a function, is that a bad
idea in terms of what it will do to the user? Should I make the user
give me two cs objects (and then check that they actually access the
same data)?

I am trying to write some functions that will bridge certain gaps
between an analysis done on a cdf that overlaps another cdf in terms of
what probes are included in each (but differ in what groups/units probes
are assigned to as well as having probes in one that aren't in the
other) and I'm suddenly wondering what I might be doing!

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] setCdf and caching
messages.body_plain:
On Feb 12, 2008 1:19 PM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> I was just wondering, if I am frequently changing the cdf for a
> AffymetrixCelSet am I going to run into any problems with something that
> has been cached? Is it better to make duplicate objects with their own
> cdf? setCdf(cs,cdf) actually takes a bit of time, so it's probably
> better for that reason.

There are two types of caching: i) in memory cache and ii) in file
cache.  The code should be careful enough to detect if you change CDF;
the getChipType(..., fullname=TRUE) is used as one of the object used
to generate the unique cache key.  I'm quite sure I went through and
checked this.  Also, when you call setCdf() on the set and in turn
each file (that's why it takes time), clearCache() in each object
should be called.  That in turn is responsible to clear all in-memory
cached results.

>
> Similarly, if I call setCdf(cs,cdf) within a function, is that a bad
> idea in terms of what it will do to the user? Should I make the user
> give me two cs objects (and then check that they actually access the
> same data)?

This definitely sounds like a potential trap for bugs and mistakes.
So some effort in protecting against such errors is needed.

>
> I am trying to write some functions that will bridge certain gaps
> between an analysis done on a cdf that overlaps another cdf in terms of
> what probes are included in each (but differ in what groups/units probes
> are assigned to as well as having probes in one that aren't in the
> other) and I'm suddenly wondering what I might be doing!

Is this something done orthogonal to actual data?  You basically
compare two CDFs?  If you could write the function to take two CDF
objects, that should be safer (and maybe clearer?).  For instance, we
already have:

identical(x,y) for all R objects
all.equal(target, current) for all R objects
equals(this, other) for all R.oo Object:s
compare(this, other) for comparing two AffymetrixCdfFile:s

Hope this helps

Henrik

>
> Best,
> Elizabeth
>
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
On Feb 12, 2008 2:55 PM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hi Henrik,
> I have a question about what you sent.
>
> >> Similarly, if I call setCdf(cs,cdf) within a function, is that a bad
> >> idea in terms of what it will do to the user? Should I make the user
> >> give me two cs objects (and then check that they actually access the
> >> same data)?
> >>
> >
> > This definitely sounds like a potential trap for bugs and mistakes.
> > So some effort in protecting against such errors is needed.
> >
> >
> Sorry, I'm not sure what you mean by this -- that either one is a bad
> idea? Or just the second idea? If I set the cdf within the function,
> will this change the cdf in the global environment? (Normally that's not
> what happens to changes within R functions)

No, it won't change anything in the *global environment*, but if you
have a AffymetrixCelSet 'cs' and call a function that does setCdf() on
that object, the new CDF *will* remain after returning (*or being
interrupted*).  Thus, a method with the side effect of changing the
CDF might be confusing.   If you use setCdf() in a method, I recommend
that you use:

foo <- function(this, ...) {
  oldCdf <- getCdf(this);
  on.exit({
     if (!identical(oldCdf, getCdf(this))) {
        setCdf(this, oldCdf);
     }
  })

  newCdf <- ...
  setCdf(this, newCdf);
  ...
}

The above will "guarantee" that your method returns having the old CDF
set regardless if the methods normally or by an error.  Note, there
will always be the risk that the user press Ctrl+C while resetting the
CDF via the last setCdf().  Then the reset will not be complete.  I
guess that could be controlled for that further by using a
tryCatch(setCdf(this, oldCdf), interrupt=function(intr) {
throw("Failed to reset CDF before returning due to a requested
interrupt.")}).

>
> Unfortunately, what I want to do is not orthogonal to the data. It's
> taking the results from a plm (e.g. chip effects) and applying them, in
> a certain sense, to additional data not used in the plm fitting. The
> additional data comes from the other cdf file, which indexes different
> probes.

So, you can uniquely infer the 2nd CDF from the 1st?

/Henrik

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] FIRMA Scores
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason.

Many of your questions will be answered when the FIRMA paper comes
out, which'll hopefully be soon (the revision is being resubmitted
next week I think).

But, basically, you are looking for large-in-magnitude FIRMA scores,
so high positive or high negative.  FIRMA scores are summaries of the
residuals (default: median) by probeset after a robust RMA model
fit ... for a given gene.  Statistical interpretation of FIRMA scores
is still somewhat of an open question, but they are at least on a
normalized scale and so should be comparable across genes ... and/or
you should be able to look at the distribution of FIRMA scores and
look for ones that stand out.

As for looking across groups/treatments, I usually do the simplistic
thing of using limma directly on the FIRMA scores and looking for
differences between groups.  That certainly has highlighted some
interesting genes for me.

Note: I/we have found it fairly important to look at the probe-level
data in combination with the residuals and FIRMA scores, as there are
specific cases where large residuals can be misleading.

I have a few scripts that might be useful to you.  Elizabeth might
have some ready-made ones also.

Hope that helps.
Mark

> example(cfit.matrix)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Simulate data
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> N <- 1000

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Simulate genotypes
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> g <- sample(c("AA", "AB", "AB", "BB"), size=N, replace=TRUE)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Simulate concentrations of allele A and allele B
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> X <- matrix(rexp(N), nrow=N, ncol=2)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> colnames(X) <- c("A", "B")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> X[g == "AA", "B"] <- 0

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> X[g == "BB", "A"] <- 0

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> X[g == "AB",] <- X[g == "AB",] / 2

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Transform noisy X
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> xi <- matrix(rnorm(2*N, mean=0, sd=0.05), ncol=2)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> a0 <- c(0,0)+0.3

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> A <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.8), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> A <- apply(A, MARGIN=2, FUN=function(u) u / sqrt(sum(u^2)))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Z <- t(a0 + A %*% t(X + xi))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Add noise to Y
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> eps <- matrix(rnorm(2*N, mean=0, sd=0.05), ncol=2)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Y <- Z + eps

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> layout(matrix(1:4, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> xlab <- "Allele A"

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> ylab <- "Allele B"

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> lim <- c(0,6)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> plot(X, xlab=xlab, ylab=ylab, xlim=lim, ylim=lim)
Waiting to confirm page change...

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> points(Z, col="blue")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> points(Y, col="red")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> legend("topright", pch=19, pt.cex=2, legend=c("X", "Z", "Y"), col=c("black", "blue", "red"), title="Variables:", bg="#eeeeee")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # Fit model
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> # - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> alpha <- c(0.10, 0.075, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01, 0.001)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> fit <- cfit(Y, dump=2, alpha=alpha, q=2, Q=98)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Ms <- fit$M

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> col <- terrain.colors(length(Ms))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> #col <- rainbow(length(Ms))
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> col[length(Ms)] <- "red"

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> lim <- c(-0.5,5)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> plot(Y, cex=0.8, xlab=xlab, ylab=ylab, xlim=lim, ylim=lim, main="Y")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> for (kk in seq(along=Ms)) {
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+   M <- Ms[[kk]]
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+   points(M, pch=19, cex=2.5, col=col[kk])
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+   lines(M, col=col[kk], lwd=2)
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+   text(M, cex=0.8, labels=kk)
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+ }

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> legend("topright", pch=19, pt.cex=2, legend=c(alpha, "final"), col=col, title=expression(alpha), bg="#eeeeee")

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> apex <- which.min(apply(M, MARGIN=1, FUN=function(u) sum(u^2)))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> a0hat <- M[apex,]

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Ahat <- M[-apex,]

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Ahat <- apply(Ahat, MARGIN=2, FUN=function(u) u / sqrt(sum(u^2)))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> if (sum(Ahat[c(1,4)]^2) < sum(Ahat[c(2,3)]^2)) {
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+   Ahat <- matrix(Ahat[c(2,1,4,3)], nrow=2)
cft.mt <http://cft.mt>+ }

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Ainv <- solve(Ahat)

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> Xhat <- t(Ainv %*% (t(Y) - a0hat))

cft.mt <http://cft.mt>> cat("True A:\n")

messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Thu, Feb 14, 2008 at 11:49 AM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  Hi,
>  I am running a plm fitting of ExonRmaPlm(...,mergeGroups=FALSE) that was
>   interrupted previously. It's being run in BATCH mode, so I was looking
>  at the output as it goes along and I see this error in the midst of the
>  processing:
>
>    Fitting probe-level model...done
>               used (Mb) gc trigger  (Mb) max used  (Mb)
>    Ncells  1371147 73.3    2251281 120.3  2251281 120.3
>    Vcells 10043983 76.7   31488280 240.3 31488171 240.3
>    Storing probe-affinity estimates...
>     Updating units...
>      Encoding units...
>      Encoding units...done
>     Updating units...done
>    Storing probe-affinity estimates...done
>    Storing chip-effect estimates...
>  <simpleError in if (regexpr(pattern, header$identifier) == -1) {
>  throw("Rcache file format error. Invalid identi
>  fier: ", file)}: argument is of length zero>

You've spotted a typo/bug in R.cache.  The error is trying to us a
connection object ('file') instead of the 'header$identifier'.  Next
release of R.cache will have this fixed.  However, this does not
explain why R.cache tries to throw an exception in the first place.
Read on...

>     Updating 132 chip-effect files...
>      Array #1 of 132 ('0124')...
>      Array #1 of 132 ('0124')...done
>
>  Should I be worried about this? The program didn't stop and seems to be
>  going along its merry way. But I'd rather stop it, destroy the previous
>  results from the stopped session, and start fresh than have question
>  mark results...

According to the above, the internal file identifier is not valid.
This could occur if the file exists but is not completely written, or
there is a racing problem in the OS's write/read cache (not R.cache),
a racing problem in a shared file system on a LAN (but that is less
likely?!?).

However, since the above occurred for an Rcache file object, I
wouldn't worry at all.  If aroma.affymetrix fails to read from file
cache, then it is the same as if it wasn't in the file cache and the
package will regenerate the data.

/Henrik

>
>  Thanks,
>  Elizabeth
>
>  >
>

Probably it's safest to get any data possible using cell indices (which

Best,
Elizabeth

Henrik Bengtsson wrote:
> On Feb 12, 2008 2:55 PM, Elizabeth Purdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Hi Henrik,
>> I have a question about what you sent.
>>
>>
>>>> Similarly, if I call setCdf(cs,cdf) within a function, is that a bad
>>>> idea in terms of what it will do to the user? Should I make the user
>>>> give me two cs objects (and then check that they actually access the
>>>> same data)?
>>>>
>>>>
>>> This definitely sounds like a potential trap for bugs and mistakes.
>>> So some effort in protecting against such errors is needed.
>>>
>>>
>>>
>> Sorry, I'm not sure what you mean by this -- that either one is a bad
>> idea? Or just the second idea? If I set the cdf within the function,
>> will this change the cdf in the global environment? (Normally that's not
>> what happens to changes within R functions)
>>
>
> No, it won't change anything in the *global environment*, but if you
> have a AffymetrixCelSet 'cs' and call a function that does setCdf() on
> that object, the new CDF *will* remain after returning (*or being
> interrupted*).  Thus, a method with the side effect of changing the
> CDF might be confusing.   If you use setCdf() in a method, I recommend
> that you use:
>
> foo <- function(this, ...) {
>   oldCdf <- getCdf(this);
>   on.exit({
>      if (!identical(oldCdf, getCdf(this))) {
>         setCdf(this, oldCdf);
>      }
>   })
>
>   newCdf <- ...
>   setCdf(this, newCdf);
>   ...
> }
>
> The above will "guarantee" that your method returns having the old CDF
> set regardless if the methods normally or by an error.  Note, there
> will always be the risk that the user press Ctrl+C while resetting the
> CDF via the last setCdf().  Then the reset will not be complete.  I
> guess that could be controlled for that further by using a
> tryCatch(setCdf(this, oldCdf), interrupt=function(intr) {
> throw("Failed to reset CDF before returning due to a requested
> interrupt.")}).
>
>
>
>> Unfortunately, what I want to do is not orthogonal to the data. It's
>> taking the results from a plm (e.g. chip effects) and applying them, in
>> a certain sense, to additional data not used in the plm fitting. The
>> additional data comes from the other cdf file, which indexes different
>> probes.
>>
>
> So, you can uniquely infer the 2nd CDF from the 1st?
>
> /Henrik
>
>
>
>> Best,
>> Elizabeth
>>
>>
>>>
>>>> Best,
>>>> Elizabeth
>>>>
>>>>
>>>>
>>>
>
> >

On Feb 14, 8:58 pm, Mark Robinson <mrobin...@wehi.EDU.AU> wrote:
> Hi Jason.
>
> Many of your questions will be answered when the FIRMA paper comes
> out, which'll hopefully be soon (the revision is being resubmitted
> next week I think).
>
> But, basically, you are looking for large-in-magnitude FIRMA scores,
> so high positive or high negative.  FIRMA scores are summaries of the
> residuals (default: median) by probeset after a robust RMA model
> fit ... for a given gene.  Statistical interpretation of FIRMA scores
> is still somewhat of an open question, but they are at least on a
> normalized scale and so should be comparable across genes ... and/or
> you should be able to look at the distribution of FIRMA scores and
> look for ones that stand out.
>
> As for looking across groups/treatments, I usually do the simplistic
> thing of using limma directly on the FIRMA scores and looking for
> differences between groups.  That certainly has highlighted some
> interesting genes for me.
>
> Note: I/we have found it fairly important to look at the probe-level
> data in combination with the residuals and FIRMA scores, as there are
> specific cases where large residuals can be misleading.
>
> I have a few scripts that might be useful to you.  Elizabeth might
> have some ready-made ones also.
>
> Hope that helps.
> Mark
>

>
>
>

> > Jason

AllelicCrosstalkCalibration class and the cfit() of 'sfit' so that we
can get more verbose output.  I've uploaded these updates as patches.

library(aroma.affymetrix)
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")

acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs)

messages.body_plain:
I am really puzzled with this one.  Everything looks right, but it
seems like the external call to 'sfit' either fails or does not
complete, because when trying to read for "pipe", there is nothing
there.  What is your operating system, Windows XP Professional,
Windows Vista, ...?  Also, under what privileges are you running this,
admin, super user, safe user?

If you don't have the right to run everything that could explain it.
However, since it worked with the bare-bone example(cfit.matrix), that
is an unlikely explanation though.

I wonder if there are some side effects from loading aroma.affymetrix
that cause the problem.  What if you do:

library(aroma.affymetrix)
library(sfit)
example(cfit.matrix)

Would that still work?

I have one more thing we could try, and I think it is worth
understanding what goes wrong, and I'm sure the answer is "obvious"
when we find it.  I'll return to you with that 2nd test, but I'll run
some torturing tests on my WinXP machine to see if I can push it to
give an error.

FYI, if you've got the data calibrated for crosstalk on your Linux
machine, you should be able to use that output (copy the files or use
the same shared directory) on Windows.  The package will detect that
the files are already there and skip the fitting (meaning it will
never call 'sfit').

/Henrik

Sorry I forget to mention I am admin user of XP professional system.

Yue

On 2/15/08, Henrik Bengtsson <h...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:

>
> I am really puzzled with this one.  Everything looks right, but it
> seems like the external call to 'sfit' either fails or does not
> complete, because when trying to read for "pipe", there is nothing
> there.  What is your operating system, Windows XP Professional,
> Windows Vista, ...?  Also, under what privileges are you running this,
> admin, super user, safe user?
>
> If you don't have the right to run everything that could explain it.
> However, since it worked with the bare-bone example(cfit.matrix), that
> is an unlikely explanation though.
>
> I wonder if there are some side effects from loading aroma.affymetrix
> that cause the problem.  What if you do:
>
> library(aroma.affymetrix)
> library(sfit)
> example(cfit.matrix)
>
> Would that still work?
>
> I have one more thing we could try, and I think it is worth
> understanding what goes wrong, and I'm sure the answer is "obvious"
> when we find it.  I'll return to you with that 2nd test, but I'll run
> some torturing tests on my WinXP machine to see if I can push it to
> give an error.
>
> FYI, if you've got the data calibrated for crosstalk on your Linux
> machine, you should be able to use that output (copy the files or use
> the same shared directory) on Windows.  The package will detect that
> the files are already there and skip the fitting (meaning it will
> never call 'sfit').
>
> /Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Ok, now we're definitely on to something.

I've updated the cfit.matrix() patch to also show the contents of the
temporary data file generated.  Please download the patches again:

library(aroma.affymetrix)
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")

Then, try the following so we can rule out a few things...

Test #1: (Repeated calls)

library(aroma.affymetrix)
library(sfit)
example(cfit.matrix)
for (kk in 1:10) {

  fit <- cfit(Y, dump=2, alpha=alpha, q=2, Q=98, verbose=TRUE)
}

Does that given an error?  If not, proceed...

Test #2: (Fitting with a much larger data set)

# Number of data points (N=1000 in the cfit example).
N <- 2e6

# Simulate genotypes

g <- sample(c("AA", "AB", "AB", "BB"), size=N, replace=TRUE)

# Simulate concentrations of allele A and allele B

X <- matrix(rexp(N), nrow=N, ncol=2)

colnames(X) <- c("A", "B")

X[g == "AA", "B"] <- 0

X[g == "BB", "A"] <- 0

X[g == "AB",] <- X[g == "AB",] / 2

# Transform noisy X

xi <- matrix(rnorm(2*N, mean=0, sd=0.05), ncol=2)

a0 <- c(0,0)+0.3

A <- matrix(c(0.9, 0.1, 0.1, 0.8), nrow=2, byrow=TRUE)

A <- apply(A, MARGIN=2, FUN=function(u) u / sqrt(sum(u^2)))

Z <- t(a0 + A %*% t(X + xi))

# Add noise to Y

eps <- matrix(rnorm(2*N, mean=0, sd=0.05), ncol=2)

Y <- Z + eps

str(Y)

for (kk in 1:10) {

  fit <- cfit(Y, dump=2, alpha=alpha, q=2, Q=98, verbose=TRUE)
}

Does this give an error?

Test #3: (Back to your data again)
With this new patch revealing even more output, retry with

process(acc, verbose=-55)

It should give an, but what is the output?

/Henrik

Hi Dong,
I don't know if this answers your question (Henrik can respond to the
implementation question), but all results in aroma.affymetrix that are
saved to .cel files are saved as 2^x (the 'intensity scale') regardless
whether this is a logical scale for the values. This is true even when
(as with Rma) the original calculations are done in the log2 scale --
the answers are converted to 2^ for storage to be consistent with this
rule. So the residuals, chip-effects, weights, probe-affinities, etc.
all need to be logged if you want them back on the standard scale in
which they were calculated.

messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] RmaPlm() in aroma.affymetrix vs. rma() in affy package
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

On Fri, Feb 15, 2008 at 12:59 PM, Dong Fu <dongf...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>  Hello Henrik,
>
>  What is the difference between your RmaPlm() function in
>  aroma.affymetrix vs. rma() in affy package?

The RmaPlm class is doing probe summarization only, which means
fitting the same log-additive model that the complete RMA pipeline is
doing in one of its steps.   RmaPlm fits the model using the
'preprocessCore' packages (formerly part of the 'affyPLM' package),
which is written by Ben Bolstad.  Ben also wrote the internal code for
rma() in the 'affy' package, but I do not know if the preprocessCore()
and the 'affy' package gives different estimates, but if they do they
should be minor.

See also:

  http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/redundancy-tests

>
>  We noticed that the results from the RmaPlm() function is not in log2
>  scale.  Is there a implementation difference?

No.  The model is fitted on the log2 scale, but we translate the
parameter estimates back to the original/intensity scale, because that
is the most generic scale on which we can compare estimates from other
model, e.g. the MbeiModel.  You could imagine some models gets
non-positive estimates on the intensity scale, then comparing on the
log-scale would not work, which is why we use the intensity scale as
the our common grounds.  The multiplicative model (MBEI; dChip; Li &
Wong 2001) is conceptually very similar to the log-additive model but
the fit is done in the intensity space.

We also do one more thing.  For all models that models chip effect and
probe affinities (as the above two), we rescale the probe affinities
to multiply to one on the intensity scale.  This corresponds to the
constraint of have probe affinities sum to zero on the log scale.
When rescaling the probe affinities with one constant this way, that
"remainder" scale the chip effects in the other direction.  But note,
all this is doing is changing a scale factor which is not identifiable
in the first place (hence the constraint) and has no impact on your
relative measures what so ever.  The latter is fundamental to
microarray analysis and important to understand.

There are more on:

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/probe-level-modelling

Now with the above, we can now compare MBEI and RMA estimates directly:

# Some units of interest
units <- 1:10000;

plm1 <- RmaPlm(csN);  # Log-additive model
ces1 <- fit(plm1, units=units);

plm2 <- MbeiPlm(csN);  # Multiplicative model
ces2 <- fit(plm2, units=units);

theta1 <- extractMatrix(ces1, units=units);
theta2 <- extractMatrix(ces1, units=units);

plot(theta1, theta2, xlim=c(0,2^12), , ylim=c(0,2^12)); # intensity scale
plot(log2(theta1), log2(theta2), xlim=c(0,12), ylim=c(0,12)); # log scale

Convenient, ehe?

Hope this makes sense

/Henrik

>
>  Thanks.
>
>  Dong
>
>
>
>  >
>

At least, the law of elimination took as a bit closer.  Yet again, do:

library(aroma.affymetrix)
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")

then

options(troubleshoot="saveAll", troubleshootPrefix="fileA")

and call process(acc, verbose=-55).

You will now get three (compressed) files in the working directory
[getwd()] that saved the state of the function and the data:

fileA01.Rbin
fileA02.txt
fileA03.Rbin

The first two are the largest and about 5-10MB each.  If you can make
these available on a webserver, please do that and let me know the
URLs.  Otherwise, email them to:

 hb-large [at] braju [com] com

I'll see if I can reproduce the problem given those files.

/Henrik

>
> >> But, basically, you are looking for large-in-magnitude FIRMA scores,
> >> so high positive or high negative.  FIRMA scores are summaries of the
> >> residuals (default: median) by probeset after a robust RMA model
> >> fit ... for a given gene.  Statistical interpretation of FIRMA scores
> >> is still somewhat of an open question, but they are at least on a
> >> normalized scale and so should be comparable across genes ... and/or
> >> you should be able to look at the distribution of FIRMA scores and
> >> look for ones that stand out.
>
> >> As for looking across groups/treatments, I usually do the simplistic
> >> thing of using limma directly on the FIRMA scores and looking for
> >> differences between groups.  That certainly has highlighted some
> >> interesting genes for me.
>
> >> Note: I/we have found it fairly important to look at the probe-level
> >> data in combination with the residuals and FIRMA scores, as there are

messages.body_plain:
Yeah, that was Elizabeth's idea actually.  It's true that we only
want to fit the PLMs for the genes contained in the Ensembl CDF, but
it makes sense to use data from the whole chip to normalize and BG
adjust the data.  That's why we did it.

It's not necessary, you could just use the Ensembl CDF the whole way
through.  I haven't compared it to see how much difference it makes.
My guess is small.

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jason,
It depends what you mean as necessary. As Mark says, for a certain
analysis we did the normalization and BG correction on all of the
main-design probes and then switched to the Ensbl to do the probe-level
model. So it's optional, in the sense that you could use the Ensbl cdf
from the beginning; the main reason we didn't do that was that then only
probes that are in that cdf are normalized and BG corrected, so if you
wanted to look at additional probes they wouldn't be corrected values.
So that depends on your analysis whether it's important to you.

But another question you might be asking is whether you could just stick
with the main design cdf for the entire analysis. Technically you *can*
(obviously) but it would not be recommended by us. The algorithm will be
very much thrown off by the level of non-expressed probesets that would
be added to any particular gene/transcript cluster. This is true also
for Affymetrix's algorithm(s). The reasons are multiple, but one reason
is that adding all of the non-expressed probesets available in the main
design would break any robust fitting algorithm (like RMA's or Affy's
Plier) to be able to do this -- and your chip effect estimates would be
lousy. The other reason, which is more important, is that the algorithm
assumes that unless the probeset is alternatively expressed, the
expression levels of the chips are parallel across probes -- the
different probe affinities only cause linear shifts (this is the linear
model fit by RMA); probesets that as a whole don't do this are called
alternatively expressed. But the non-expressed probesets generally will
have a very different behavior than the expressed probesets and so will
be called as alternatively spliced: lots of false positives. The better
your annotation, the less false positives this will give.

However, if you are just getting probeset estimates (mergeGroups=FALSE)
from the linear fitting then you can use the main-design cdf all the way
through.

On the otherhand, if you like having Affy's transcript clusters, you
could use the 'core' probesets and probably do okay. We like the Ensembl
cdf better because how Affy clusters probesets together results in
stringing a some genes together, while we tend to throw more of those
out, I think (as well as noting when they occur in the names we give the
unit. Ultimately we found it easier to stick to one carefully done
annotation; while core are 'reliable' probesets, they are still from
multiple sources which are combined together algorithmically by Affy.
Even combining RefSeq transcripts (a main annotation in core) into gene
definitions seems difficult, based on talking to someone who did it,
while Ensembl is more straightforward.

Best,
Elizabeth

This took a bit longer than I anticipated, but it still do the job.
After each chunk you should see an estimate of ETA and how much time
spent for reading, fitting, and writing.  Unfortunately, writing takes
quite some time, but what percentage do you get?

Also, it is typically much faster to process the data on a local drive
than over a file network, but I'm not sure if you've got the option to
do it locally.

>
> So is there a way to have the RmaPlm pick up from where it left off?
> Or do we need to start from scratch?  I found that in the plmData
> folder there are a lot of processed data files already.

It picks up where it ended.  In each chunk, first the probe affinities
are saved, then the chip effects array by array.  The fit() function
look at the last array to decide what units need to be fitted, e.g. if
the R session is interrupted while writing, it will refit that whole
last chunk.

I've used the above many times; for instance running it on one
machine, then interrupt R in order to move the processing to another.

> > (about 580 out of 676 chunks done).
>
> This took a bit longer than I anticipated, but it still do the job.
> After each chunk you should see an estimate of ETA and how much time
> spent for reading, fitting, and writing.  Unfortunately, writing takes
> quite some time, but what percentage do you get?
>
> Also, it is typically much faster to process the data on a local drive
> than over a file network, but I'm not sure if you've got the option to
> do it locally.

Forgot to mention, there is also an argument 'ram=1' that fit() takes
- it is a "scale" factor and if you set  'ram' > 1, more units are
fitted per chunk (using more memory of course), which could save you
some of the I/O overhead.

/Henrik

>
> >
> > So is there a way to have the RmaPlm pick up from where it left off?
> > Or do we need to start from scratch?  I found that in the plmData
> > folder there are a lot of processed data files already.
>
> It picks up where it ended.  In each chunk, first the probe affinities
> are saved, then the chip effects array by array.  The fit() function
> look at the last array to decide what units need to be fitted, e.g. if
> the R session is interrupted while writing, it will refit that whole
> last chunk.
>
> I've used the above many times; for instance running it on one
> machine, then interrupt R in order to move the processing to another.
>
> /Henrik

On Feb 18, 2008 9:33 AM, Dong Fu <dongf...@gmail.com> wrote:

Yes, with a small disclaimer.  So, the QN is done using a two-pass
scan of the data.  In the first scan, the target/baseline distribution
is identified.  This roughly "sums" the arrays and saves the "average"
in a target distribution file.  So, if R is interrupted during this
first pass, it has to be redone all over.  In the second pass, each
array is normalized to the target distribution, i.e. it is a
single-array normalization method at this stage.  Any arrays already
normalized will be skipped.  An array is considered normalized if
there exist an output file (the probeData/ one you refer to).  Now to
the catch, the output data is current saved in two lines of code:

  createFrom(this, filename=pathname, path=NULL, verbose=less(verbose));
  updateCel(pathname, intensities=x);

The first one, createFrom(), creates an empty CEL file and the second
one writes the normalized data to that file.  I have taken greate care
of making the first one "atomic", i.e. it either returns a valid CEL
file or not.  Now, if the R session is interrupted after createFrom()
but before updateCel() [in affxparser] is complete, the result will be
a CEL files only partially populated.  updateCel() is rather fast so
the risk is not that big, but still there.

It is on my todo list to make the above two calls as one "atomic"
call, i.e. either you get a CEL file with normalized data or you
don't.  In the meanwhile, you can delete the last CEL file written in
the probeData/...,QN/ directory to be on the safe side.

> On the other hand, I will do the RmaBackgroundCorrection
> before doing the QN part this time, so maybe I need to redo this
> anyway.

Yes, I remember you question on how well aroma.affymetrix replicates
rma().  If you to a small-set comparison, I would be great if you
could share your findings here.

>
> So if I did not get to save the results of the CelSet loading from
> ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A"),
> do I also need to load them again?

I'm not sure what you mean by "save" here, but I might guess.
Basically the 'ds' object, which is of class AffymetrixCelSet, holds a
list of AffymetrixCelFile objects which each holds a pathname to the
CEL file (plus some other minor fields).  That is all.  The above
fromName() static method call will locate the CEL set and scan the
directory for CEL files and rebuild this structure.  Since you have
5000+ arrays, this might take a substantial time for you, is that
right?  In that case, you can use the file cache mechanism to do
something like this:

 force <- FALSE;
 key <- list(method="fromName", class="AffymetrixCelSet",
                name="myDataSet", tags=NULL, chipType="HG-U133A");
 dirs <- "myCacheDir";
 ds <- loadCache(key, dirs=dirs);
 if (force || is.null(ds)) {
   ds <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", chipType="HG-U133A");
   saveCache(ds, key=key, dirs=dirs);
 }

This will cache the result in getCachePath(dirs=dirs) and you don't
have to worry about where you save it and what file name you use.  the
(key, dirs) pair makes it unique.

Basically, I could add a 'force=TRUE' argument to fromName() and put
everything inside to do exactly that - this is what is done in many
places where a method is computational expensive.  But I first have to
see if there are any side effects, before I do that.

>
> I will remember to save more often all the intermediate results as
> they all take a long while to generate.

You can also load normalized data directly by specifying the data set tags, e.g.

  csN <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("myDataSet", tags="QN", chipType="HG-U133A");

and process from there.

Hi Elizabeth and Mark,

Thank you both so much for your replies. That has made things a lot

On Feb 18, 4:55 pm, Elizabeth Purdom <epur...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Jason,
> It depends what you mean as necessary. As Mark says, for a certain
> analysis we did the normalization and BG correction on all of the
> main-design probes and then switched to the Ensbl to do the probe-level
> model. So it's optional, in the sense that you could use the Ensbl cdf
> from the beginning; the main reason we didn't do that was that then only
> probes that are in that cdf are normalized and BG corrected, so if you
> wanted to look at additional probes they wouldn't be corrected values.
> So that depends on your analysis whether it's important to you.
>
> But another question you might be asking is whether you could just stick
> with the main design cdf for the entire analysis. Technically you *can*
> (obviously) but it would not be recommended by us. The algorithm will be
> very much thrown off by the level of non-expressed probesets that would
> be added to any particular gene/transcript cluster. This is true also
> for Affymetrix's algorithm(s). The reasons are multiple, but one reason
> is that adding all of the non-expressed probesets available in the main
> design would break any robust fitting algorithm (like RMA's or Affy's
> Plier) to be able to do this -- and your chip effect estimates would be
> lousy. The other reason, which is more important, is that the algorithm
> assumes that unless the probeset is alternatively expressed, the
> expression levels of the chips are parallel across probes -- the
> different probe affinities only cause linear shifts (this is the linear
> model fit by RMA); probesets that as a whole don't do this are called
> alternatively expressed. But the non-expressed probesets generally will
> have a very different behavior than the expressed probesets and so will
> be called as alternatively spliced: lots of false positives. The better
> your annotation, the less false positives this will give.
>
> However, if you are just getting probeset estimates (mergeGroups=FALSE)
> from the linear fitting then you can use the main-design cdf all the way
> through.
>
> On the otherhand, if you like having Affy's transcript clusters, you
> could use the 'core' probesets and probably do okay. We like the Ensembl
> cdf better because how Affy clusters probesets together results in
> stringing a some genes together, while we tend to throw more of those
> out, I think (as well as noting when they occur in the names we give the
> unit. Ultimately we found it easier to stick to one carefully done
> annotation; while core are 'reliable' probesets, they are still from
> multiple sources which are combined together algorithmically by Affy.
> Even combining RefSeq transcripts (a main annotation in core) into gene
> definitions seems difficult, based on talking to someone who did it,
> while Ensembl is more straightforward.
>
> Best,
> Elizabeth
>
> Jas wrote:
> > Hi Mark,
>
> > Thanks for the code. That helps heaps.
> > I notice that you change cdfs to Ensbl, after normalization and before
> > fitting the probe level model.
> > I  have just one question, is this necessary or have you done this
> > just for convenience, so that you have the gene names rather than the
> > Affy transcript numbers?
> > Thanks again,
>
> > Jason
>
> > On Feb 17, 1:02 pm, Mark Robinson <mrobin...@wehi.EDU.AU> wrote:
>
> >> Hi Jason.
>
> >> Apologies for the delay.  I've attached a script that does all the

>
> >>> Thank you so much for your reply and I look forward to reading the
> >>> paper when it comes out.
> >>> Could you please email me the scripts you spoke of (jas074 at
> >>> gmail.com <http://gmail.com>)? I would be extremely grateful if you did.
> >>> Thanks again for your help, that certainly gives me ideas as to how to
> >>> proceed.

>
> >>> On Feb 14, 8:58 pm, Mark Robinson <mrobin...@wehi.EDU.AU> wrote:
>
> >>>> Hi Jason.
>
> >>>> Many of your questions will be answered when the FIRMA paper comes
> >>>> out, which'll hopefully be soon (the revision is being resubmitted
> >>>> next week I think).
>
> >>>> But, basically, you are looking for large-in-magnitude FIRMA scores,
> >>>> so high positive or high negative.  FIRMA scores are summaries of the
> >>>> residuals (default: median) by probeset after a robust RMA model
> >>>> fit ... for a given gene.  Statistical interpretation of FIRMA scores
> >>>> is still somewhat of an open question, but they are at least on a
> >>>> normalized scale and so should be comparable across genes ... and/or
> >>>> you should be able to look at the distribution of FIRMA scores and
> >>>> look for ones that stand out.

> >>>> thing of using limma directly on the FIRMA scores and looking for

Skip the getData() method - it's intended for developers only.
Instead, use extractMatrix() or extractDataFrame().  Make sure to
download the latest patches or the latter before you continue, i.e.

library(aroma.affymetrix)
downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")

Example:

> theta <- extractMatrix(ces, units=1:100)
> theta[1:4,1:3]

[2,] 192.8629  79.34032  72.93121
[3,] 174.8281  61.75642  57.05348
[4,] 376.7764 175.37138 180.99246

> data <- extractDataFrame(ces, units=1:100, addNames=TRUE)
> data[1:4,1:8]
        unitName groupName unit group cell   array1    array2    array3
1 AFFX-BioB-5_at              1     1    1 110.8957  49.07429  54.76605
2 AFFX-BioB-M_at              2     1    2 192.8629  79.34032  72.93121
3 AFFX-BioB-3_at              3     1    3 174.8281  61.75642  57.05348
4 AFFX-BioC-5_at              4     1    4 376.7764 175.37138 180.99246

> stopifnot(identical(unname(theta), unname(as.matrix(data[,-(1:5)]))))

Yes, the above values are on the intensity scale so you have to log them, e.g.

ltheta <- log2(theta)
ldata <- cbind(data[,1:5], log2(data[,-(1:5)]))

Alternatively, you bring the rma estimates to the intensity scale.

Hope this helps

messages.body_plain:
Hi Valeria,

On Feb 19, 2008 12:52 PM, vesp...@inmegen.gob.mx

<vesp...@inmegen.gob.mx> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Can someone tell me if it is possible to access the common reference
> file created and used during the cbs method. Is it possible to use it as
> a reference in  an other  data set?

Example:

seg <- CbsModel(cesFln);
fit(seg, chromosome=22);
refTuple <- getReferenceSetTuple(seg);
refSet <- getListOfSets(refTuple)[[1]];
refFile <- getFile(refSet, 1);
yRef <- getData(refFile, fields="intensities")$intensities;

The above applies to any segmentation method, e.g. GladModel and CbsModel.

Explanation: all segmentation models in aroma.affymetrix can combine
data from multiple chip types.  The working term for a *list* of CEL
sets is a *CEL set tuple*.  For each chip type there is a reference,
either a single file or a set of files.  In the case of a single file,
we still consider the reference as a set of files (the same file
replicated multiple times).  So,

  refTuple <- getReferenceSetTuple(glad)

first extract the tuple of CEL set references (contains one or more
CEL sets).  Since we know there is only one, we extract that one:

  refSet <- getListOfSets(refTuple)[[1]]

This is a (Cn)ChipEffectSet.  In the above case, it contains the same
reference file replicated nbrOfArrays(cesFln) times.  We get this by:

  refFile <- getFile(refSet, 1)

This is a (Cn)ChipEffectFile, e.g.

> refFile
CnChipEffectFile:
Name: .average-intensities-median-mad
Tags: 01ecc75622a8ca3d584335148e1465cd
Pathname: plmData/Jeremy_2007-10k,ACC,-XY,RMA,+300,A+B,FLN,-XY/Mapping10K_Xba142
/.average-intensities-median-mad,01ecc75622a8ca3d584335148e1465cd.CEL
File size: 445.83kB
RAM: 0.01MB
File format: v4 (binary; XDA)
Chip type: Mapping10K_Xba142,monocell
Timestamp: 2008-01-24 20:10:47
Parameters: (probeModel: chr "pm", mergeStrands: logi TRUE, combineAlleles: logi
 TRUE)

As you see, it is actually a regular CEL file, but hidden away and
with a hashcode part of the filename.

The best way to get the probe signals is (for now):

  yRef <- getData(refFile, fields="intensities")$intensities

Hope this helps

/Henrik

> Valeria

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nancy,

On Feb 19, 2008 11:34 PM, Nancy <nrz...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,  I am processing a great number of cancer samples using the Hapmap
> samples as reference.  In the command,
>
> plm.as <http://plm.as> <- AvgCnPlm(csC, ...)
>
> is it possible to use previously estimated probe affinities ( e.g.
> from the reference set ) to process the test set?   I get the cancer
> samples a few at a time and so don't want to re-estimate the probe
> affinities every time a new cancer sample is fit.

Did you mean RmaCnPlm(), because all AvgCnPlm() is doing is estimating
the robust average across all probe intensities.  In the chip
effect/probe affinities worlds this corresponds to fixing all probe
affinities to one.

So, first for the RmaCnPlm, unfortunately you cannot reuse the probe
affinities.  This idea has been raised many times, especially for
large data sets.  It has been on the todo list almost from the very
beginning, but it never makes it up to the top before something else
pushes it down.

Back to the AvgCnPlm.  This is not really a two-way model with chip
effects and probe affinities because the latter are all ones.  A
two-way model is a multi-array model, whereas the AvgCnPlm model is a
single-array model.  However, due to lack of time, I utilized the
RmaCnPlm framework to implement AvgCnPlm, which means that in practice
"fits" the model across array (probeset by probeset).  Thus, the real
solution will be to reimplement AvgCnPlm to do the "fit" for each
array separately.  Which would solve your problem.  [Thus, with
allelic crosstalk calibration and an updated summarization
implementation, the method is truly single-array up to that point].
...on my todo list.

It is also on my todo list to speed up the processing by identifying
all single-probe unit groups and simple "fit" those by taking the chip
effect as the probe intensity.  For the GWS5/GWS6 that would speed up
things quite a bit since half of the units are CN probes.

/Henrik

>
> Thanks!  -Nancy
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Feb 20, 2008 at 12:26 PM, vesp...@inmegen.gob.mx
<vesp...@inmegen.gob.mx> wrote:
>
>  Hi.
>
>  I ran the PCR fragment length normalization. It gave me 38 warnings, all
>  involving NaNs being produced

> "Is it normal to receive these warnings."

Yes, that is alright.  These warnings are because the allelic
crosstalk in the first place introduces a tiny set of non-positive
values (typically for the homozygote SNPs and expected), and although
summarization makes this set even smaller, some do end up as
non-positive chip-effect estimates.   Now, since the fragment-length
normalization is done on the log-scale, the negative ones obviously
become NaN:s (and the zero ones -Inf).

In general, warnings are just to make you aware of a condition (like
"FYI").  Errors are always errors and should never be ignored.

/Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] can I analyze custom array?
messages.subject_clean: [aroma.affymetrix] can I analyze custom array?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jin,

the answer to the question in the subject line is, sure.  One of the
design goals with aroma.affymetrix is that is should work with custom
CDF with minimal setup.

On Thu, Feb 21, 2008 at 7:24 AM, JP <playb...@yahoo.com> wrote:
>
>  Hi Henrik,
>
>  We have made custom SNP array for mouse (similar to SNP5). I have a
>  bunch of CEL files and a custom CDF.  I really hope to utilize
>  aroma.affymetrix to conduct copy number analysis.  Would you please
>  offer some hints?

First of all, since you mentioning the similarity SNP5 chip type, I
want to make sure you understand the different between the "default"
and the "alternative" CDFs of the SNP chip type.  For the latter, each
CN probe is in its own unit, whereas in the former, several CN probes
are bundled together in the same unit.  You want your CDF to have one
CN probe per unit.   This does not affect the SNP units, where you
have multiple probes per allele pair and multiple strands.

Second, make sure you work with a binary version of your CDF, because
an ASCII CDF simply be too slow to work with.  You can use
convertCdf() in affxparser to convert an ASCII CDF to binary format.

So from you other message sent offline I know that you want to CN
analysis.   With CEL files and a CDF file - but no other annotation
files - you can do all of the following:

library(aroma.affymetrix)
verbose <- Arguments$getVerbose(-8)
timestampOn(verbose)

cdf <- AffymetrixCdfFile$fromChipType("MusCGDm520547_01")
print(cdf)

cs <- AffymetrixCelSet$fromName("MyDataSet", cdf=cdf)
print(cs)

acc <- AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(cs, subsetToAvg=NULL)   # NOTE
print(acc)
csC <- process(acc, verbose=verbose)

plm <- AvgCnPlm(csC, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, shift=+300)
print(plm)
fit(plm, verbose=verbose)

ces <- getChipEffectSet(plm)
print(ces)

More below.

>  When I tried to use aroma, I was able to input data
>  but then got the following error:
>
>  +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
>  +++++
>  Error in list("process(acc)" = <environment>,
>  "process.AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(acc)" = <environment>,  :
>
>  [2008-02-21 09:25:57] Exception: Failed to retrieve genome information
>  for this chip type: MusCGDm520547_01
>   at throw(Exception(...))
>   at throw.default("Failed to retrieve genome information for this
>  chip type: ", chipType)
>   at throw("Failed to retrieve genome information for this chip type:
>  ", chipType)
>   at getGenomeInformation.AffymetrixCdfFile(cdf)
>   at getGenomeInformation(cdf)
>   at getSubsetToAvg.AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(this)
>   at getSubsetToAvg(this)
>   at getParameters.AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(this)
>   at getParameters(this)
>   at process.AllelicCrosstalkCalibration(acc)
>   at process(acc)
>  +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
>  ++++++

The reason for this error is because by default
AllelicCrosstalkCalibration use argument subsetToAvg="-XY", which says
that it should fit the model parameters using all chromosomes but X
and Y.  In order to infer what loci are on what chromosomes,
additional annotation data beyond the CDF is required, namely genomic
locations for each unit (loci).  In my example above, I circumvent
this by saying all units can be used to fit the model, which is
suboptimal.  Instead...

You will need to setup a so called Unit Genome Position (UGP)
annotation file which contains  a (unit, chromosome, position) map
specific to given CDF.  If you have a NetAffx containing this
information, you can follow the instructions on how it was done for
the GenomeWideSNP_6,Full.cdf:

 http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/genomewidesnp-6---miscellaneous

If you don't have a NetAffx-like data file, you can still allocate an
empty UGP file, e.g.

ugp <- AromaUgpFile$allocateFromCdf(cdf, tags="JP20080221");
print(ugp)

and populate the UGP map yourself, e.g.

#  Set the chromosomes for the first seven units
ugp[,1] <- c(1,1,2,2,3,4,5)

#  ...and their physical positions
ugp[,2] <- c(13410,43031,10322,10323,34303,12304,40335)

Note that the rows in the UGP table should map one-to-one to the units
in the CDF, e.g.

unitName <- "SNP_A-123231"
unit <- indexOf(cdf, unitName)
stopifnot(getUnitNames(cdf, unit), unitName)

...and the genome position for this unit should be:

print(ugp[unit,])

You will also need the UGP for doing the segmentation later on.

Similarly, if you want to do the fragment-length normalization (as
suggested in the vignette), also need to create a Unit Fragment Length
(UFL) annotation file for your custom CDF.   I'll leave that for now,
but the idea is very similar, cf.

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/building-ufl-file-for-genomewidesnp-6

>
>  We were able to use apt-probeset-genotype to obtain raw intensities
>  (Plier). Is there a way to input these intensity data?

There are some notes on this at:

http://groups.google.com/group/aroma-affymetrix/web/import-from-affymetrix-power-tools-apt

Yet again, you will still need UGP annotation data in order to proceed
to the segmentation step.

Finally, as a group member, you're welcome to write up your own notes
in a Subpage to 'Documentation on chip types' (under "Pages") for your
custom chip type/CDF.  There you can also show how you create the UGP
etc.

Hope this helps you get started.

/Henrik

PS. Since this message already contains many different topics, for
future messages, please use a separate thread/subject line for each
topic. DS.

>
>  Thanks so much!

>  Jin

Hi Nancy.

On Thu, Feb 21, 2008 at 11:33 AM, Nancy <nrz...@gmail.com> wrote:

>  samples, but if the batch contain *only* cancer samples, would the
>  probe level estimates in copy number variant regions be wrong?

Your chip-effect estimates will be standardized towards the robust
average of all arrays.  That's is basically true for all probe-level
summarization models.  In other words, your chip effects will be
relative to the average cancer sample.

>
>  So I tried grouping the cancer samples with some normal samples to be
>  analyzed together.  But the cancer samples use the Early Access 100K
>  array, while the normal samples are the regular 100K array.  Can these
>  two be analyzed together?  Or, maybe I'm wrong and don't need to worry
>  about this...

No, unfortunately you cannot mix two different chip types in
probe-level summarization.

The only way I can see how this could be done is to identify all
probes that are in common in the two chip types and only work with
those, and ignore all other probes in the summarization step.   In
order to do this, you will need to create a custom CDF for this
"joint" chip type, and then transform all CEL files to map to this new
CDF by reshuffling the probes.  To minimize the amount of work for
this, the probe indices in custom CDF can be chosen to map to the main
chip type (say Mapping50K_Hind240) and then you only have to reshuffle
the CEL files for the Early Access version.  All bits and pieces for
doing this is available in aroma.affymetrix and affxparser, but in
order to do it, you have to know quite a bit about how CEL and CDF
files work.

Another alternative is fit the 100K cancer samples and the EA100K
normal samples separately (if you got enough of them), and combine
them on the chip-effect level.  Say 'ces' and 'cesEA' are
CnChipEffectSet estimates for the 100K and the EA100K chip type.  Then
you can extract chip effects as:

data <- extractDataFrame(ces, addNames=TRUE)
dataEA <- extractDataFrame(cesEA, addNames=TRUE)

[until next release is available, you have to install patches for this
to work, i.e. downloadPackagePatch("aroma.affymetrix")]

Then you have to match the unit names in the two sets - data$unitName
and dataEA$unitName, and ignore all other units.  Next step is to
bring the two sets of estimates to the same scale.  The most basic,
and a bit naive approach, is to use quantile normalization  to do
this.   In aroma.light (sic!), there is a normalizeQuantile() that
takes a matrix (rows are units and columns arrays) and returns a
normalized matrix of the same shape.  That could work.

If you want to proceed with aroma.affymetrix segmentation methods, you
then face the problem to get that data back into a format recognized
by the package.  This basically bring you back to the custom CDF
problem (not completely, but similarly).   Otherwise, you use the
DNAcopy and/pr GLAD package standalone.

Cheers

Henrik
